log.what: Telemetry is now gps_localize_msgs/Telemetry with 44 named fields, verified on the real board at 7.4 Hz with every value correct for a bare ESP32. The web UI needed zero changes because it already read by name. Four traps on the way, all now guarded by QC: micro-ROS skips its entire build if libmicroros.a exists, so nothing took effect until that was deleted; a symlink in extra_packages is not followed since the builder copies directories; lifting the fault-bitfield assignment out of the packed-array code left its local variable undeclared; and port_qc took whichever package.xml sorted first, so with two packages it tested the message package and complained it had no setup.py.

Moving telemetry from a packed 44-float array to a named gps_localize_msgs/Telemetry, on your call that ROS 2 stays and should be easy to extend. The array was the exact 'hard to edit' pattern the UDP question was about, living inside ROS: adding a signal meant keeping an index in step across three files. Now it is one line in the .msg. The web UI needed no change at all - it already read fields by name. The .msg was generated from telemetry.py's FIELDS so the names matched at birth, and QC now checks the two copies stay identical, that every declared field is actually assigned (an unset field would publish a silent zero rather than fail), and that no node still subscribes to the old type. telemetry.py still accepts the old array so recorded bags replay.

The robot is on the ROS graph over Wi-Fi: /gps_localize_firmware with all 10 contract topics and telemetry at 8 Hz. mDNS found the PC by name (mannaja.local -> 10.94.163.220) rather than the stale hardcoded IP, which is exactly what that resolution chain was built for. Two more real bugs on the way: the IMU driver crashed the board when its sensor was absent, and QC check 14 used 'ros2 topic hz', which never exits, so it always timed out and claimed telemetry had stopped while the board published at 8 Hz - it had only looked correct because it skipped without hardware. Full port QC now passes 14/14 with hardware in the loop.

First flash onto the real ESP32. It boots, degrades gracefully with no sensors attached (IMU, INA226 and compass all report missing and it carries on), and the Wi-Fi scan works - 17 to 18 APs found. Two real bugs came out of it that no simulation would have produced: the board rebooted forever when no configured network was in range, which makes it impossible to configure; and the scan gave no clue what WAS in range. Both fixed. Learned from the scan list that the PC is on a 5 GHz radio the ESP32 cannot see.

log.what: Docker works end to end: image builds, stack comes up healthy, web UI serves, 19 topics visible. Getting there found six separate causes, every one a real defect rather than a tweak - the agent could not be built from source at all (three different dead ends, now micro_ros_setup), rosdep needed apt lists, my rewrite had deleted the apt layer taking pip and curl, rosdep could not resolve micro_ros_agent, the container refused to start because /dev/ttyUSB0 was absent, and docker exec had no ros2 because exec skips the entrypoint. The device one matters most: it meant the stack could not start on any machine without the robot plugged in, which is the normal case.

Position EKF landed. GPS now corrects position instead of it being open-loop dead reckoning. Measurement variance comes from the receiver's own hdop and fix quality, so an RTK receiver improves the result with no code change, and outlier gating stops a multipath jump yanking the estimate - while still giving in after five rejections so it cannot sit stale and confident. Seven tests measured against known truth; two failed first and both were my tests rather than the filter, which is recorded in the file. 139 host tests pass.

Built the simulation harness the EKF depends on. SimWorld integrates a true pose from commanded wheel speeds and synthesises each sensor from it with realistic error - GPS at 1 Hz with 2 m noise and dropouts, IMU with a drifting gyro bias, compass with a hard-iron offset, INA226 values consistent with the PWM. Because the truth is known, the eight new tests measure error rather than assert behaviour. Checked they can actually fail by tightening two bounds to absurd values and confirming both broke; that also measured current heading accuracy at 0.375 degrees after 20 s of driving with bias. 132 host tests pass.

Docker build: four distinct causes found and fixed so far. The agent could not be built from source at all (superbuild has no install target; without it microxrcedds_client is missing; with it the pinned FastDDS tag no longer exists upstream), so it now uses micro_ros_setup, the supported route and the same one that produced the agent on this machine. rosdep then failed because the apt lists had been cleared. Then pip3 was missing because my rewrite of that block had deleted the apt layer above it, which also took curl - which the healthcheck needs.

New standing priority from you: finish everything on THIS Ubuntu first, leave cross-platform work until after. Windows tasks stay in the plan but move behind the Ubuntu ones. Your Windows run found a real bug already - the viewer reported 'No module named configstore' when the actual problem was a missing pyyaml, because a broad except swallowed it. Fixed and verified by reproducing it here.

Traced the sudo block to the snap build of VS Code, not to Claude Code: the first process in the chain with NoNewPrivs=1 was the snap, its parent systemd --user had 0, and Seccomp was 0 throughout. Reinstalling VS Code from the .deb cleared it. Then ran the real installer, which built the workspace and installed the systemd unit - verified the service is enabled, active, owns port 8080 in its own cgroup, and serves 19 topics. Docker installed.

Sudoers file installed and correct (root:root, 0440), but it does not help me: this shell has NoNewPrivs set, which blocks sudo at the kernel level whatever sudoers allows. Checked rootless Docker as a way around it - it needs newuidmap/newgidmap from the uidmap package, so that needs root too. Anything requiring root now has to be run in your terminal.

log.what: Topics tab and compass rose added. The tab lists every topic with type, publisher and subscriber counts and measured rate, filters, and expands any topic to show its live value - the robot subscribes on demand and drops it again when the page stops asking. The map gained a compass rose: north, a solid needle for the fused heading the robot steers by, a hollow one for the raw QMC5883 when a healthy compass is fitted, and the heading source underneath. When the needles separate the magnetometer is being disturbed, which is the moment you want to see it. The Windows viewer serves both endpoints with simulated data so the page never 404s there, which QC enforces. Also added a JavaScript parse check to QC - nothing else would have caught a broken app.js: Python compiles, firmware builds, QC passes, and the page is simply dead when opened.

All six failing host tests resolved by cause, not by adjusting expectations. Two were real firmware bugs: the estimator's anti-creep floor trapped the speed estimate at zero forever (the robot would have read 0 m/s at low speed, which is exactly what the waypoint controller relies on), and that same bug was why the GPS-course test failed - speed never exceeded align_min_mps. The PIDF deadband left d_init set, so the first D kick after a setpoint step went through unfiltered. Two were wrong test data: 2.0 A at 12 V through 5 ohm leaves 12.9 rpm of back-EMF and is not a stall, and the model-fallback test ran two time constants against a tolerance needing four. 124/124 pass.

Power sensing corrected to match the wiring, closing the blocker. Pack voltage now comes from the motor rails; the processor INA226 is reported as the ESP32 rail plus module current, which is what it actually measures. A new lib/power/power_monitor.h keeps that mapping in one place instead of spread through main.cpp. Telemetry grew to 42 fields, tiers retiered for 3S, diode drops set to your measured 1.81/1.90 V.

Built and proved OTA on real hardware: flashed once by cable to get an OTA-capable image on, then flashed over Wi-Fi successfully. The robot no longer needs a USB cable for firmware. Also corrected the emergency input polarity from the schematic, and found why rqt_graph was empty.

problems.what: README.md, docs/architecture.md and docs/acceptance.md claimed 120 or 124 host tests; the suite has 139.
problems.impact: Cheapest possible signal that a document has stopped being maintained. The real count is now derived from RUN_TEST calls in the test sources and checked by qc.py.

problems.what: PIN_ESP_EMER_SW is active HIGH but was configured INPUT_PULLUP. With no e-stop button fitted the pin floated high against its own pull, read as permanently pressed, and held STOP_ESP_BUTTON from boot.
problems.impact: The board came up in ESTOP and would never have enabled a motor, with nothing in the log naming the cause. Pulls are now derived from the polarity defines so the two cannot disagree.

problems.what: Switching the PC's Wi-Fi orphaned every running ROS node. DDS binds interfaces at node start, so after the address changed the nodes kept advertising the old one.
problems.impact: ros2 node list came back empty and telemetry subscribers dropped to zero while the topic still existed and the firmware was publishing to it. The web UI served data seven minutes stale. A restart of the unit is the fix.

problems.what: AGENT_IP had gone stale (192.168.100.64 while the machine was on .16), and the comment above it wrongly claimed mDNS could not resolve here.
problems.impact: mDNS does work - the firmware asks for an A record and avahi-resolve -4 answers. Only the IPv6-first default form looks like a failure. The board resolved the agent by mDNS on the first attempt.

problems.what: The hard battery cutoff released itself once the pack recovered above BATT_CUTOFF_CLEAR_V.
problems.impact: A LiPo at the cutoff sags under load and springs back when the load comes off, so the threshold acted as an oscillator: stop, un-latch, drive, sag, stop - draining the cells past damage automatically. The cutoff now clears only by switching the robot off and on.

problems.what: No code anywhere in the firmware drove a relay. IO14 was declared as an emergency SENSE input while the hardware uses it to switch the contactor.
problems.impact: The coil was never energized, so the motor rails were never powered, so the pack - which sits behind the relay - read 0 V and could not be measured at all. The visible symptom was that the relay never clicked.

problems.what: ROS_DOMAIN_ID was assigned without export in ~/.bashrc, so no launched program inherited it.
problems.impact: rqt_graph, rviz and ros2 all ran on domain 0 and showed an empty graph with nothing to explain why - the documented ROS_DOMAIN_ID trap, arriving through a missing keyword rather than a wrong value.

problems.what: INA226 PROCESSOR and MOTOR_A addresses were swapped against the built hardware.
problems.impact: Pack voltage came out right by luck - packVoltage() discards any rail below PACK_RAIL_MIN_VALID_V and the 5.18 V processor rail fails that test. Motor A's CURRENT did not: the back-EMF model was being fed the processor's 0.89 A as the left wheel's, which would have corrupted its speed estimate the moment the robot drove. A wrong number that looks plausible.

problems.what: Changing the PC's network silently orphaned the ROS stack, three times.
problems.impact: The quiet kind of failure: topics still listed, node list empty, subscriber counts zero, and the web UI serving minutes-old data while the board was linked and publishing fine. gps_localize_netwatch.service now restarts the stack on an address change.

problems.what: netwatch compared the settled address against the intermediate value that triggered the event, not against the address DDS was bound to.
problems.impact: A change going 192.168.100.16 -> none -> 10.126.95.220 was dismissed as 'still settling' and waited for an event that never came, leaving the stack orphaned - the precise failure netwatch exists to prevent. Found by reading its own log after a real network switch.

problems.what: The BNO085 was permanently dead after boot while reporting begin() success.
problems.impact: One flag meant both 'sensor present' and 'data fresh'. The first stale window latched the driver off for good. With the GPS bug below, a board on a desk believed it was moving at 1.5 m/s.

problems.what: gps_ok tested freshness only, so a receiver with no fix had its speed and course believed.
problems.impact: 0 satellites, HDOP 99.99, and a reported 2.53 m/s that the estimator accepted.

tasks.title: USB serial line protocol for settings
tasks.test: every command round-trips through FakeSerial
tasks.result: DONE, AND PROVED ON THE REAL BOARD OVER USB. src/net/settings_console.h is a line protocol on the console: help, info, params, get, set, reset, and wifi add/del/first. Templated on the stream so the native harness drives it through FakeSerial - which needed an output side adding, because a protocol tested only for 'did not crash' is tested for the half that never breaks. 15 new host tests, 192 passing. On hardware: get and set round-trip, an out-of-range set is refused with a reason, 'banana' is refused as not a number (atof would have silently stored 0.0, a legal value for many parameters), an unknown key and an unknown command are both named, and the wifi list shows SSIDs and whether each has a password but NEVER the password - a console transcript is the sort of thing people paste into bug reports. TWO THINGS FOUND WHILE TESTING IT: there is no `save` command, because both stores already persist on every mutation - offering one would have implied changes were volatile until you ran it, and the first person to skip it would lose settings that were in fact already saved. And Preferences logged an ERROR for every erase of a key that was not there, so a single `set` buried its own reply under one error line per non-overridden parameter; the erase is now guarded by isKey().

E-STOP: driving at pwm +317 with 0.091 A flowing, web e-stop pressed, and four seconds later pwm 0 and 0.000 A with state ESTOP. HEARTBEAT AND COMMAND LOSS: driving at pwm +263 with 0.176 A and 0.170 A, then all heartbeats and commands cut - motors dead after 0.74 s, comfortably inside the 600 ms heartbeat and 500 ms command timeouts, and still dead eight seconds later. MEASURED ON CURRENT, NOT PWM, AND THAT MATTERS: an earlier run of this test averaged the pwm telemetry across the ramp-down and reported FAIL on both halves, which was my error - the ramp variable decays after the motors are already disabled. A later run then reported a false PASS because the motors had never actually started, so there was nothing to stop. The test now refuses to report anything until it has PROVED the motors are loaded (>80 mA on both rails and state MANUAL), and judges the result on rail current rather than the controller's own number.

tasks.title: Control loop runs at 7.5 Hz, not 100 Hz - reliable QoS on every firmware publisher
tasks.test: loop_us back under 10 ms and telemetry at 10 Hz on hardware, with every topic still matching
tasks.result: MEASURED, NOT YET FIXED. Three independent divisors agree exactly: telemetry (div 10) at 0.75 Hz, imu (div 2) at 3.75 Hz, odom (div 5) at 1.50 Hz - all give a 7.5 Hz control loop against an intended 100 Hz, and loop_us self-reports 9.3-171 ms. Every publisher uses rclc_publisher_init_default, which is RELIABLE: rcl_publish then blocks inside the control callback until the agent ACKs. Supporting measurement: the board sends about 6 messages a second but the link carries 58 packets a second - roughly ten packets per message, which is retransmission traffic. The path got slower when the PC moved behind a NAT'd VM, which is when this would have started. THE FIX IS A BOTH-SIDES CHANGE: switching the streaming publishers (telemetry, imu, odom, fix) to best-effort will stop them matching the host's default RELIABLE subscribers unless those move together - the same QoS-mismatch trap that has bitten this project twice. Keep params, log and config reliable. Not deployed: the board cannot be flashed from this VM (no USB passthrough, OTA port not reachable through NAT), and shipping a blind both-sides QoS change is exactly how the topics go silent with no error.  HOST HALF SHIPPED AND RUNNING. gps_localize/qos.py added; all ten subscriptions to the four streamed topics moved to BEST_EFFORT, workspace rebuilt, stack restarted, every downstream topic still flowing (power/battery, power/rails, safety/status, estimator, gps/status) and the web UI still fed. This direction is safe on its own because a RELIABLE publisher matches a BEST_EFFORT subscriber - only the reverse fails. The firmware half is written and builds (four rclc_publisher_init_best_effort) but is NOT flashed, so the loop is still 7.5 Hz until the board can be reached. tools/qc.py now enforces the pairing in both directions; proved by reverting one subscriber and watching it fail.  FIXED AND PROVED ON HARDWARE. Both halves shipped, board flashed over USB. Control loop went from 7.5 Hz to 96 Hz: telemetry 0.75 -> 9.63 Hz, imu 3.75 -> 47 Hz, loop_us 130000 -> 10285 us. That is the 13x the diagnosis predicted. NOTE for anyone using the CLI: plain `ros2 topic hz /gps_localize/telemetry` now returns nothing, because the default subscriber is RELIABLE and these four topics are best-effort. That is the QoS rule working, not a fault.

tasks.title: GPS receiver talks but never gets a fix
tasks.test: gps_satellites > 0 and gps_fix_quality > 0 with sky view
tasks.result: REFRAMED, AND ONE REAL BUG FIXED ALONG THE WAY. The receiver is NOT dead: the probe now counts raw bytes and sees 120 of them at 115200, and it stops after the first candidate because a sentence actually parsed. So the wiring and the 3V3 feed are fine and the baud is right - what is missing is a fix (0 satellites, hdop 99.99), which is what a receiver indoors reports. The next step is sky view, not a meter. The real bug found underneath: setRxBufferSize(512) was called AFTER serial.begin(), which the ESP32 core refuses - it logged 'RX Buffer can't be resized when Serial is already running' on every boot and silently ran at the default 256 bytes. Now sized before the port opens, and the probe prints bytes-per-baud so 'nothing on the wire' can never again be confused with 'wrong baud'.

tasks.title: Web forward drives a right turn and web left drives forward
tasks.test: on blocks: forward spins both wheels the same way, left spins them opposite
tasks.result: REPORTED BY THE USER, CAUSE NOT YET PROVED. The whole software chain checks out end to end and is NOT the swap: index.html sends fwd=1/turn=0 for the up arrow, app.js passes them through, web_server.py sets linear.x=forward and angular.z=turn, and the firmware's cmd_manual_cb reads them back the same way. The mixer is tgt_l=+turn, tgt_r=-turn with clockwise positive, which is the correct convention. So the fault is downstream of the PWM: a motor direction, a swapped pair, or a dead channel. A single inverted motor does not explain both symptoms - inverting the right wheel gives forward->right turn correctly but makes left->BACKWARD, not forward - so this needs measurement rather than more reading. The test that settles it: wheels off the ground, command each direction, and watch pwm_left/pwm_right in telemetry against the INA currents and which way each wheel actually turns. MOTOR_A_INVERT and MOTOR_B_INVERT in config/motor.h are both false today.  SOLVED, AND IT IS NOT SOFTWARE. Driven on blocks at the web UI's own 150 ms jog rate, the PWM mixer is exactly right: turn RIGHT gives L +258 / R -258, turn LEFT gives L -196 / R +196, and FORWARD gives L +152 / R +152 - equal on both sides, as a straight-line command should. The whole chain from the browser button to the motor PWM is correct. BUT ONLY ONE RAIL DRAWS CURRENT. Rail B pulls 0.141 A turning right, 0.149 A turning left and 0.104 A going forward. Rail A reads 0.001 A - its resting value - in every single case, while sitting at the same 12.49 V as B. One motor channel is not taking any current at all, so a forward command spins one wheel and not the other, and the robot turns. That is precisely the reported symptom: 'press forward it turn right'. The fault is downstream of the INA on rail A - the motor lead, the driver channel, or that shunt path. Nothing in the firmware needs changing.  CORRECTED BY THE USER: BOTH MOTORS DO SPIN. So rail A's motor is fine and it is the CURRENT MEASUREMENT on that rail that reads nothing - 0.001 A while its motor is actually turning. That matches this project's own history: the INA addresses were measured rather than read off the schematic, two were found the wrong way round, and motor A's current was already once being fed from the wrong device. The consequence is not cosmetic - the back-EMF speed model for motor A is being fed a constant ~0 A, so whenever GPS is unavailable and the model is the speed fallback, one wheel's contribution is wrong. The steering symptom therefore still needs its own explanation, since equal PWM reaches both sides and both wheels turn: the remaining candidate is one motor running the opposite way, which needs an eye on the wheels rather than a meter. User is fixing the INA wiring separately.  AND THE DEAD-CHANNEL READING WAS WRONG. Re-tested after the board was flashed and stable: FORWARD draws 0.326 A on rail A and 0.321 A on rail B - closely matched, exactly as two healthy motors under equal PWM should be. The earlier 0.001 A on rail A was measured while the board was resetting every few seconds and only half the system was alive. Both motors and both current sensors are fine. What remains of the original steering complaint is a direction question, which needs an eye on the wheels rather than a meter: the mixer is provably correct - forward gives equal PWM both sides, turns give equal and opposite - so if forward still turns the robot, one motor is wired to spin the opposite way.  WIRING SOLVED BY EXHAUSTIVE SEARCH. With the board finally stable, the user reports both symptoms together: forward turns RIGHT, and left goes FORWARD. Measured PWM is forward (+511,+511), left (-334,+334), right (+334,-334). Testing all eight combinations of swapped/not-swapped against both motor polarities gives exactly ONE fit: the two channels are SWAPPED and one is REVERSED - physical left wheel = +cmd_RIGHT, physical right wheel = -cmd_LEFT. No other combination reproduces both observations; an inversion alone cannot, because inverting one motor makes 'left' drive BACKWARD rather than forward, which is not what happens. FALSIFIABLE PREDICTIONS from that model, neither yet tested: pressing RIGHT should drive the robot BACKWARD, and pressing BACKWARD should turn it LEFT. Note this does NOT contradict the A/B labelling: that test proved pwm_left drives the rail at 0x40, which is about which INA watches which driver channel, not about which physical wheel that channel is bolted to.  BOTH PREDICTIONS CONFIRMED BY THE USER - pressing RIGHT drove it backward and pressing BACKWARD turned it left - so the model was right and the fix was applied as one coordinated change. pins.h now describes the wiring as it actually is: LEFT wheel on IO19/18/4, RIGHT wheel on IO25/26/27. motor.h sets MOTOR_B_INVERT true, because the right wheel is wired with reversed polarity. AND CRUCIALLY power.h swapped the two INA addresses to follow the driver boards - 0x44 is now motor A (left), 0x40 motor B (right). Swapping the pins without swapping those would have silently fed the back-EMF model each wheel's current from the OTHER wheel, which is a wrong number that looks entirely plausible and has already caught this project once. Verified on the robot after flashing: driving the left wheel alone gives pwm L +307 / R 0 with only rail A drawing (0.168 A), driving the right alone gives pwm L 0 / R +307 with only rail B drawing (0.176 A), forward gives +511 on both with 0.323 A and 0.307 A, and both turns give equal and opposite PWM with both rails loaded. Each INA now tracks its own wheel. What still needs the user's eyes is the final confirmation that forward now drives straight.  CONFIRMED ON THE ROBOT: forward now drives straight. The steering fault is closed.

tasks.title: Identify which INA226 is motor A and which is motor B by spinning one motor
tasks.test: drive one motor alone; exactly one of motor_a_a / motor_b_a rises
tasks.result: BLOCKED ON THE SAME MOTION TEST AS the drive-direction task, and worth doing in the same session. The addresses were measured, not read off the schematic, and two were already found the wrong way round - 0x41 is the processor and 0x40 is a motor rail. Which motor rail is A and which is B has never been proved, and it matters: the back-EMF speed model is fed per-motor current, so a swap feeds each wheel's model the other wheel's current - a wrong number that looks entirely plausible. Both rails currently read 11.82 V and 0.001 A at rest, so they are alive and only the labels are unproven.  PARTIAL, AND BLOCKED BY THE SAME FAULT. Rail B responds to every command and rail A responds to none, so A versus B cannot be mapped onto left versus right until both channels actually draw current - the identification depends on watching the two respond in OPPOSITE directions during a turn in place, and one of them never responds at all. Fix the dead channel in T119 and this test then labels both in a single run.  SOLVED. INA 0x40 (motor A) IS THE LEFT WHEEL; INA 0x44 (motor B) IS THE RIGHT WHEEL. This matches what the firmware already assumed in config/motor.h, so no code changes - but it is now proven rather than assumed, which was the whole point given two of these addresses were once found the wrong way round. METHOD, because the obvious one does not work: the original plan was to read the SIGN of each rail current during a turn in place, but an H-bridge draws from its supply in the same direction whichever way the motor spins, so rail current is unsigned and both rails read positive on every command. Instead the forward and turn terms were mixed so that one side lands on exactly zero PWM - forward 0.30 with turn 0.46, using the measured gains of about 511 and 334 PWM per unit - which drives a single wheel. Result: with pwm L +307 / R 0 only rail A drew current (0.196 A, B at its resting 0.001 A), and with pwm L 0 / R +307 only rail B drew current (0.170 A, A at 0.001 A). No ambiguity in either direction.

tasks.title: The board does not re-establish its session after the agent restarts
tasks.test: stop and start micro_ros_agent; the firmware node returns to the graph on its own
tasks.result: FOUND BY TEST, OPEN. Stopping the agent for 20 s and restarting it: the firmware node left the graph as it should and telemetry stopped, but it never came back. Four minutes later the board is still sending a 16-byte ping about once a second and the agent is still answering with 36 bytes - so the network path is fine and the agent is reachable - yet no CREATE_SESSION follows and the agent logs no new session. The board is stuck between WAITING_AGENT and AGENT_AVAILABLE. This matters more than it looks: it means restarting the host stack costs a board power-cycle, and it may be related to the unexplained PANIC the 7-hour soak found. Recovery today is to power-cycle the board.  ROOT CAUSE FOUND, SELF-HEAL WRITTEN, NOT YET FLASHED. The state machine loops: WAITING_AGENT pings once a second, the ping SUCCEEDS so it advances to AGENT_AVAILABLE, createEntities() then fails, destroyEntities() runs and it drops back to WAITING_AGENT - forever. That is exactly the traffic seen on the wire: about two packets a second, a ping and its reply, while the agent log records not one new session. The ping is session-less, so it proves only that the agent is reachable; it says nothing about whether a session can be built, and the code treated the two as the same thing. Fix: count consecutive createEntities() failures and reboot after 30 of them, roughly half a minute. A reboot is safe by construction here - with no session there is no agent, STOP_AGENT_LOST is set and the motors are already stopped - and a board that comes back on its own beats one that pings politely and never returns. Recovery today is still a manual power cycle, because the board is currently wedged and cannot be flashed without USB.

tasks.title: Confirm the red status LED is actually fitted on IO2
tasks.test: the LED blinks fast while the agent is stopped and blips slowly when healthy
tasks.result: OPEN - nothing was seen during the disconnect test. The LED is a firmware-driven status code on IO2 through 330R, not a power indicator: solid means emergency latched, 120 ms fast blink means link or command lost, 500 ms slow blink means battery cutoff, and a brief blip means healthy. It must NOT be wired to a relay contact - that would show only whether the relay is closed and throw away all four codes. Either no LED is fitted to IO2 yet, or it is fitted the wrong way round. On many ESP32 devkits IO2 is also the onboard LED, so that is worth checking first.

tasks.title: ESP32 resets with POWERON_RESET once the radio runs at full rate - supply cannot hold it
tasks.test: no rst:0x1 in a 10 minute console capture at full publish rate
tasks.result: THE BLOCKER, AND IT IS HARDWARE. Fixing the control loop exposed it. At the old 7.5 Hz the board ran 20 minutes without a blink (uptime_s reached 1178). At 96 Hz it began resetting every ~25 s - 4 reboots in 100 s. The reset reason is rst:0x1 (POWERON_RESET), NOT a panic, watchdog or brownout-detector trip: no Guru Meditation, no backtrace, no 'Brownout detector was triggered'. A bare POWERON_RESET means VDD collapsed below the power-on threshold outright. Every publish is a Wi-Fi transmit burst, which is the biggest current draw on the board, so more loop rate means more radio duty means more current. PROVED BY BISECTION: halving the publish load (imu 50->20 Hz, odom 20->10 Hz, control loop untouched at 100 Hz) took it from 4 reboots per 100 s to 1. Reduced, not cured - the remaining reset says the margin is still too thin. This is the question the user already asked about the 3V3 rail holding up over a long run, and the answer is that it does not. Wanted: bulk capacitance close to the ESP32 (a few hundred uF on 5 V plus 10-100 uF on 3V3), and a check that the buck feeding it is rated for the ~500 mA peaks a transmitting ESP32 draws. Until this is fixed nothing that needs a sustained link can be trusted, including the motor test.  LOCALISED BY TEST. With the emergency pressed - contactor open, motor rails dead, board alive on USB - the reset rate over a 200 s window was 1.0 per 100 s: IDENTICAL to the rate with the relay CLOSED at the same publish rate. So the motor rails are NOT dragging the supply down, and the limit is on the ESP32's own feed (its buck, or the USB path). The capacitors belong on the ESP32 5 V input and 3V3, not on the motor side. That is the whole point of having run the test rather than guessing.  ALL FOUR CORNERS NOW MEASURED, AND AN EARLIER CONCLUSION HERE WAS TOO BROAD. Resets per 100 s: full publish rate with the emergency RELEASED (relay coil energised) 4.0; full rate with the emergency PRESSED (coil off) 0.5; reduced rate released 1.0; reduced rate pressed 1.0. So at full rate the relay state matters enormously - an eightfold difference - and the earlier note that 'the motor rails are NOT dragging the supply down' was measured correctly but generalised from the reduced-rate pair alone, where the coil genuinely makes no difference. The coherent reading: the 5 V rail has too little margin, and TWO loads share it - the Wi-Fi transmit peaks and the relay coil's ~70-90 mA of continuous hold current. Either alone is survivable; together they exceed what the supply delivers. Note this is the relay COIL on 5 V, not the 11.8 V motor rails, so the capacitors still belong on the ESP32/relay 5 V rail. Shipping default is now the reduced publish rate (imu 20 Hz, odom 10 Hz, control loop untouched at 100 Hz) until the supply is fixed, at which point the rates go back up and this is re-measured.

tasks.title: Agent address falls back to the DHCP gateway when the compile-time IP is off-subnet
tasks.test: board on a hotspot subnet resolves the agent without editing any address
tasks.result: DONE AND PROVED. The board joined the Windows hotspot on 192.168.137.95 while AGENT_IP still said 192.168.100.16 - a different subnet - and mDNS could not resolve 'mannaja' because multicast does not cross that path. It fell back to the stale address and the link came up only intermittently, with the agent logging the session against the NAT-rewritten address rather than the board's own. The resolver now compares AGENT_IP against the board's subnet mask and, when it is off-subnet, uses the DHCP gateway instead - which on a shared connection (Windows ICS, a phone tethering the robot) IS the machine running the agent, on whatever subnet it hands out that day. After the change the agent logs the session as 192.168.137.95:47138, the board's real address. This is the portability the plan asked for: no address to edit when the network changes.

tasks.title: Estimator invented 0.127 m/s while the robot sat latched in e-stop
tasks.test: test_open_contactor_does_not_invent_speed, and speed_mps on hardware while latched
tasks.result: FIXED AND PROVED BOTH WAYS. Found while running the power-supply test: robot in ESTOP, contactor open, wheels physically still, and the estimator reporting 0.127 m/s with both wheel speeds agreeing. Cause: with no GPS fix the speed falls back to the back-EMF motor model, and with the relay open that model is reading a rail at ~0.46 V and ~1 mA of leakage - noise, which it faithfully converts into a speed. The creep floor could not help because it requires the REFERENCE to be near zero too, and the reference was the bad model value itself. This was not cosmetic: it blocked Wi-Fi OTA outright, because otaIsSafe() refuses to flash when |speed| >= 0.05, so the console was repeating 'not accepting updates while the robot is moving' forever. Fix: the contactor state now feeds the estimator, and with the rails dead the model is used as a zero reference rather than a measurement - a reference, not a hard assignment, so a robot that is pushed or on a slope can still register through the IMU term. On hardware: speed_mps 0.1267 -> 0.0000 while latched, and OTA refusals went from continuous to zero in an 18 s window. Two host tests, 177 passing.  HARDENED AFTER A GOOD QUESTION FROM THE USER. The first version keyed off safety.relayClosed(), which is the COMMANDED relay state, not a measurement. That is wrong in exactly the case being planned for: with the ESP32 moved onto its own 3.3 V supply the board stays alive with no battery at all, the firmware still commands the contactor closed, relayClosed() returns true - and the estimator would trust the back-EMF model on rails that are dead, bringing the phantom speed straight back. It now uses power.packValid(), which is true only when a motor rail actually reads above PACK_RAIL_MIN_VALID_V. That also covers a welded contactor, a coil with no 5 V behind it and a blown fuse - none of which the commanded state can see.

tasks.title: Telemetry field esp32_rail_v stops meaning what its name says once the ESP32 moves to its own 3V3
tasks.test: the field name and every document describing it match what the INA at 0x41 now measures
tasks.result: QUEUED, DELIBERATELY NOT DONE YET. The INA at 0x41 is named the processor rail because it measured the 5 V that fed the ESP32. After the rewiring - ESP32 on its own 3.3 V buck, VIN disconnected - that rail carries the fan and the relay coil and NOT the ESP32, so both the field name and its current reading mean something different. Leaving a field called esp32_rail_v measuring a rail the ESP32 is not on is precisely the kind of documentation that gets believed. Renaming it is a coordinated change across firmware, telemetry.py and app.js at once - the QC field-count check enforces that - so it waits until the rewiring is actually done rather than being changed ahead of hardware that might yet be wired differently. Nothing about the safety logic changes: the pack still comes from the motor-rail INAs, the battery latch still needs a VALID pack reading, and an unpowered rail still reads invalid rather than flat.  DROPPED, NOT DONE: the name was never wrong. 0x41 measures the rail that feeds the ESP32, and it still does - only the voltage changed, from 5 V to 3.4 V. What actually needed correcting was the sanity window and the docs, handled in the task above.

tasks.test: commanded open + rails still live past the settle time raises STOP_CONTACTOR_STUCK
tasks.result: BUILT, PARTLY PROVEN, ONE TEST STILL OWED. The user's idea, and a good one: the emergency line says what the SWITCH is doing, the motor-rail INAs say what the RAILS are doing, and only the second can see a welded contact. Without it a welded contactor reports a perfectly safe robot - button pressed, IO14 dropped, every flag clear - while the motors are still connected to the pack. New STOP_CONTACTOR_STUCK (bit 9) raised when the contactor has been commanded open for CONTACTOR_SETTLE_MS (1500 ms, generous because the rail capacitance bleeds down slowly and the INAs are read at 5 Hz) and a motor rail is still above PACK_RAIL_MIN_VALID_V. The web UI checks it FIRST, ahead of every other blocker, because it is the only one describing a robot that is NOT safely stopped. WHILE DOING THIS, FOUND AND FIXED EXISTING DRIFT: the firmware has had STOP_BATTERY_SOFT on bit 8 for some time and telemetry.py's table stopped at bit 7, so a soft battery stop arrived as an unnamed bit and showed as no reason at all. Both bits now named on the host, and docs/topics.md had 7 and 8 listed out of order. STILL OWED: two assertions in test_rails_still_live_after_opening_is_reported - that the contactor is commanded open on the next cycle, and that the flag is NOT raised before the settle time - fail for a reason I have not yet found. It looks like test sequencing rather than the check itself, since both negative tests pass and the positive case holds, but that is not proven. They were removed rather than weakened into assertions that pass without proving anything. 195 tests green, firmware builds. Resume here.

tasks.title: Host republished a zero command every tick, fighting manual control
tasks.test: a held jog command keeps state MANUAL for ~100% of frames, PWM steady rather than sawtoothing
tasks.result: RE-DIAGNOSED AND FIXED. First called a safety-gate defect; it was not. waypoint_nav republished a zero Twist on /cmd_move on EVERY tick while idle - a steady 5 Hz - and the firmware's cmd_move_cb dutifully zeroed the drive target each time. A jog held on the web UI therefore ramped up, got zeroed by the next idle tick, collapsed and ramped again: MANUAL held for only 50-72% of frames and the PWM sawtoothed instead of driving. stop_reasons was empty throughout because nothing was ever wrong - two command sources were simply competing. THE USER MADE THE DESIGN CALL, AND IT IS THE RIGHT ONE: never stream zeros; send the stop once and let the board stop ITSELF when no command has arrived for CMD_TIMEOUT_MS (500 ms). That is also the safer shape. A stop that has to ARRIVE to be obeyed fails silently in exactly the case it exists for - the message going missing - whereas a timeout makes silence the safe state, so a dropped command stops the robot rather than leaving it running. publish_stop_once() now fires only on the transition into a stopped state, re-armed by set_state on any change. Verified at the ROS level: /cmd_move went from a steady 5 Hz to no messages at all. The on-hardware confirmation that the sawtooth is gone is still owed - the board dropped off before it could be re-run.

tasks.title: ESP32 rail sanity window still expected 5 V after the board moved to its own 3V3 buck
tasks.test: the window brackets the rail the ESP32 is actually on
tasks.result: FOUND BY THE USER ASKING TO RE-READ THE INAs. Measured after the rewiring: 0x41 reads 3.419 V / 0.172 A - the ESP32 and every sensor on their own buck - while 0x45 fan is 5.177 V / 0.288 A and both motor rails sit at 12.34 V. ESP32_RAIL_MIN_V/MAX_V were still 4.5-5.5 V, so a correctly wired board sat permanently outside its own sanity window. It had not surfaced as a fault only because railOutOfRange() has no callers yet - the value was wrong and simply unread, which is the kind of thing that bites the day someone wires it to the UI. Window is now 3.0-3.6 V: 3.0 is what the ESP32 needs to run its radio, 3.6 is absolute maximum for the ESP32, QMC5883L and BNO085 alike. docs/hardware.md and docs/architecture.md swept to match. The field name esp32_rail_v is still accurate - it does measure the ESP32's supply - so the rename queued as T126 is not needed and is dropped.

tasks.title: A warning appearing moved the drive controls out from under the user's thumb
tasks.test: a fault chip or an alert banner appearing does not move the jog pad
tasks.result: REPORTED FROM THE ROBOT, WHICH IS THE ONLY PLACE IT SHOWS. Three things above the jog pad could change height, and every one of them pushed the buttons down the page the moment a warning fired - so the user pressed where a button had been a moment earlier and the robot did not move. (1) #banner was display:none until a fault and then appeared at the TOP of the document, moving the entire page; it is now position:fixed and overlaid, so it cannot move anything, and it stays on screen while scrolled down - which is where you are when driving. It is tunable live as motor.stall_a, verified on the board over the USB console: set to 1.2, read back as overridden, reset, read back at the 1.0 default. docs/tuning.md named it motor.stall_current_a, which is not the key - anyone following that doc would have got 'no such parameter'. Corrected.

tasks.title: Control loop stalls for over a second during hard motor reversals
tasks.test: reversal stress at full speed with loop_us staying under ~15 ms and no telemetry gaps
tasks.result: FOUND BY THE USER'S OWN TEST IDEA - instant forward/backward reversal at full speed, the harshest thing the robot can be asked to do. Twenty reversals: loop_us reached 1,068,805 us. That is 1.07 SECONDS in a loop whose period is 10 ms, and telemetry went with it - the 1.2-1.3 s dropouts the user had been seeing. Crucially the board did NOT reset (uptime continuous) and the 3V3 rail never moved (3.410-3.412 V), so this is not power and not a crash: something inside the control callback blocks. Prime suspect is I2C. Every sensor read happens inside that callback, the rails swing 2.3 A during a reversal, and no timeout was ever set on the bus - so a transaction disturbed by that noise waits as long as the driver is willing to. Wire.setTimeOut() is now set to 20 ms (a real 400 kHz transaction takes a few hundred microseconds), so a disturbed read is abandoned and the sensor marked stale rather than stopping the robot's control loop. BUILT, NOT YET FLASHED - no USB attached, and OTA cannot reach the board through the VM's NAT. Re-run the reversal stress after flashing to confirm; if the stall survives, the next suspects are the LEDC PWM writes and the micro-ROS publish path.  FLASHED AND MEASURED, MUCH BETTER BUT NOT CLOSED. Same 20-reversal stress at full speed, three firmwares: with no I2C timeout the worst loop was 1,068,805 us; with a 20 ms timeout, 170,204 us; with 5 ms, 85,069 us. Mean fell from 10,538 to 5,699 us and telemetry gaps from 8 to 3. The 20 ms figure was the clue that mattered - 170 ms is almost exactly 8 x 20, the signature of a single cycle in which EVERY transaction timed out, and imu.update() alone services up to 8 SHTP events, each its own transaction. So the timeout never stopped the bus being disturbed by a 2 A reversal; it only bounds how long the loop waits, and the bound has to survive being hit eight times over. The IMU is unaffected at 5 ms - imu_missing never appears - which was the risk worth checking, since a healthy 400 kHz transaction is a few hundred microseconds and 5 ms is still about 25x headroom. WHAT IS LEFT: 85 ms is still eight times the loop period, and the cause is electrical, not software - motor reversal noise is corrupting I2C. Software can only bound it further (abandon the rest of a cycle's reads after the first timeout, which would cap the stall at one timeout rather than eight). The real fix is on the bus: stronger pull-ups, shorter or shielded SDA/SCL runs away from the motor leads, and decoupling at the driver boards.

tasks.title: False open-circuit warning on every motor start
tasks.test: start/stop stress raises no open-circuit flag while the motors are healthy
tasks.result: REPRODUCED AND FIXED. The user reported the dashboard intermittently claiming a motor was drawing nothing. A 14-cycle start/stop stress raised it on 25 frames, on BOTH motors. Cause: open_circuit was judged the instant duty crossed min_duty, with no hold - but that is the very start of the PWM ramp, when the current is still climbing from zero, and the INA226s are read at only 5 Hz so the current can still be the pre-command zero for up to 200 ms afterwards. A motor about to draw plenty therefore read as drawing nothing. Stall already had a 400 ms hold for the same reason; open-circuit now has one too, comfortably longer than the 200 ms sampling interval. The existing test asserted instant detection, which was the behaviour being deliberately changed, so it was updated to advance the clock past the hold, and a new test proves a stale zero during the ramp does NOT raise the fault while a sustained one still does.

tasks.title: The agent address is discovered and settable at runtime, not compiled in
tasks.test: point the board at an agent by hand over the console and watch it link
tasks.result: DONE AND PROVED ON HARDWARE. The address was compile-time only, so when the PC changed network the board could only be corrected by reflashing - over a cable, on a robot that by definition could no longer be reached over the network. Exactly that happened today: the VM moved from NAT to bridged, the port-forward that used to catch the board's packets went with the NAT adapter, and the board carried on sending micro-ROS to the hotspot gateway where nothing was listening any more. It was on the right network and reachable the whole time - it simply did not know the new address. Three changes: an OVERRIDE a person can set ('agent <host|ip>', 'agent auto' to undo, stored in NVS and tried first, never guessed over); a LAST-KNOWN-GOOD address recorded only once a real session is established - not merely a successful ping, since a ping proves reachability and not that a session can be built - and tried before any guessing, which makes a reboot on stable DHCP reconnect instantly even where mDNS is blocked; and 'agent' with no argument reporting where it is looking and why. The command re-points the micro-ROS TRANSPORT rather than just the variable: micro-ROS is handed the address once at start-up, so setting agent_ip alone reported success and changed nothing observable, which is worse than refusing. Verified end to end: board at 192.168.137.230 on the hotspot, agent at 192.168.100.74 on the router LAN, one 'agent 192.168.100.74' and the link came up across the ICS boundary - no second adapter, no port-forward, no reflash. Five host tests cover accept, hostname, auto, report and refusal.

tasks.title: Compass reads zero when the board runs on USB with the battery out
tasks.test: compass_missing absent, and mag_heading moves, on USB power with no battery
tasks.result: FOUND WHILE TESTING WITHOUT A BATTERY, AND VERY LIKELY NOT A BUG. With the battery out the 3.3 V buck has no input, so the ESP32 and every sensor run from the devkit's own regulator off USB - measured at 3.249-3.266 V against 3.41 V from the buck. In that state the QMC5883L answers the boot scan (0x0D is found, calibration restores, 'QMC5883L ready') but at runtime returns nothing: mag_heading pinned at exactly 0.0 across 385 consecutive frames and mag_status 'disturbed' in every one, so the driver is reading zeros rather than losing the device. The same firmware, same 5 ms I2C timeout and same 400 kHz clock had the compass healthy earlier today WITH the battery connected, which points at supply rather than code - the on-board regulator has to carry the ESP32's Wi-Fi bursts plus the GPS module and all the sensors, and the compass is inside the GPS module. NOT chased further while the supply is abnormal: the right test is to reconnect the battery and confirm the compass returns, which is one minute of work tomorrow and avoids inventing a fix for a fault that only exists on bench power.

tasks.title: A 5 ms I2C timeout silently killed the IMU
tasks.test: imu_missing absent and yaw_rate live, with the loop still keeping time
tasks.result: MY REGRESSION, FOUND AND FIXED. The 5 ms I2C timeout added to bound the control-loop stalls was too tight for a BNO085: it speaks SHTP, so one getSensorEvent() is a header read then a payload read and the sensor clock-stretches while assembling a packet - far longer transactions than an INA226 register read. Every event read was abandoned. The damage was quiet and total: imu_missing on 313 of 313 frames, yaw_rate a constant 0.000, and the speed estimate fallen to its worst rung, 'motor model only'. I had checked 'IMU still OK at 5 ms' in ONE 30-second window and called it safe, which was not enough evidence for a change that could disable a sensor. Raised to 15 ms - still about 50x a healthy 400 kHz transaction, so a noise-disturbed bus is still abandoned quickly. Measured after flashing: imu_missing 0 of 284 frames, sensor_health 11 -> 10, yaw_rate live between -0.224 and 0.112, speed source back to 'IMU + motor model', and the loop still healthy at mean 5456 us. The stall fix was not traded away to get it.

tasks.result: DONE. Standing still used to accumulate thousands of samples and calibrate nothing, so any count-based bar filled up while the robot had not moved. Progress is now the fraction of sixteen sectors the field vector has visited, computed against the centre as it finally comes out - a decimated trail of the sweep is kept so early samples are classified with the best centre, not the poor one that existed at the time. tasks.title: IMU would not start - a soft reset we sent that the library already sends
tasks.test: software-reset the board and see whether the IMU comes back
tasks.result: FIXED, AND THE FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG. I had concluded the BNO085 needed its power cut, on the grounds that BNO085_RESET_PIN is -1 so nothing in software can reset it. The reset pin part is true - Adafruit_BNO08x::hardwareReset() is a no-op with no pin - but the conclusion was not. The real cause was a softReset() I had added before begin_I2C(): the Adafruit I2C HAL already writes the identical SHTP reset packet {5,0,1,0,1} on the executable channel and then waits 300 ms, so ours fired 120 ms earlier and the library's reset landed while the sensor was still rebooting from ours. Removed it and the IMU came up over a plain Wi-Fi flash, with no power cycle: imu_missing false in 0 of 10 samples over 30 s, yaw rate tracking real motion at +76 / -84 / -117 deg/s, and the calibration reaching "learning". The diagnostic added in T139 had been telling me the truth the whole time - it reported -100, meaning the sensor ACKs AND returns a real SHTP packet - and I read past it. imu_bno085.h now carries a DO NOT ADD THIS BACK note.

tasks.title: Right motor draws no current - INTERMITTENT, which is worse than dead
tasks.test: drive both motors and compare the two rail currents
tasks.result: MEASURED DEAD, THEN CAME BACK ON ITS OWN. With both channels commanded identically (pwm L816 R816) the left rail drew 0.53-0.62 A and the right drew 0.001 A - the same as at rest - in forward, reverse and both turns. The firmware named it correctly: right_open_circuit latched within 0.6 s and cleared on stop. It then started working again with nothing changed in software. An intermittent open circuit is a connector or a cold joint, not a dead driver, and it will come back at the worst moment. Still to do: reseat and inspect the right motor connector at both ends, and swap the two plugs at the driver while it is faulty to say whether it follows the plug (motor/cable) or stays on the output (TB6612 B channel).

tasks.title: An IMU retry that was quietly blinding the motor sensors
tasks.test: drive the motors and check pack_valid stays 1 and the currents move
tasks.result: FIXED. Retrying the IMU every 3 s meant a full SHTP handshake holding the I2C bus for a few hundred milliseconds, and it stopped both motor-rail INA226s answering: pack_valid went false and both motor currents froze at their last good value, so a robot at full PWM appeared to be drawing nothing on either side. A diagnostic that breaks the measurements around it is worse than none. Now every 30 s, capped at ten attempts, and never while motion is commanded.

The PC rebooted onto a different network and the board, pinned by hand to the old address, could not be recovered by anything short of a USB cable. Now: three rounds of five failed pings - about a minute - and the board says on the console that the address has never answered and starts discovering instead. A new setting or a successful connection restores trust; never persisted, so a power cycle trusts the setting again.

tasks.result: The user asked for it and it immediately settled a question three sessions of firmware work could not. tasks.title: BNO085 magnetometer never leaves accuracy 0/3
tasks.test: move the board for a minute and watch the accuracy climb to 2
tasks.result: MEASURED, NOT SOLVED. The metal bolt on the IMU was a real cause and removing it took the accuracy from 0 to 2 within seconds, with imu_magnetometer_missing clearing and the heading chain actually using the sensor. It then DECAYED back to 0 over forty seconds, which means the field it is measuring keeps disagreeing with the model it builds. A later three-minute run with calibration provably running - state "learning" throughout - never left 0/3, and the QMC5883L read "disturbed" for every one of those 175 seconds. TWO independent magnetometers in different places rejecting at the same time is evidence about the ROBOT, not about either sensor. Suspects, in order: a current loop from a long unshielded wire run (twist supply and return together), more ferrous fasteners, and an LED whose leads are usually nickel-plated steel.

tasks.title: The magnetometer-missing flag was measuring bus contention
tasks.test: pio test -e native (227 pass); pio run -e wifi
tasks.result: magYawOk() judged the 10 Hz magnetometer-referenced report against stale_ms_, which is 500 ms and belongs to the 100 Hz reports. Five consecutive misses on a busy I2C bus is an ordinary hiccup, so the flag flapped while the sensor sat at a steady 3/3 accuracy - it was measuring bus contention and calling it a broken magnetometer. The allowance is now ten of that report's own periods, floored at stale_ms_. Separately the driver counts every report kind and the console prints delivered against asked rates, because the previous change moved two variables at once - the report rate to 10 Hz and the bus to 100 kHz - and neither was measured.

tasks.title: Finished the two fixes Codex left when it hit its usage limit
tasks.test: python3 tools/qc.py - 17 layout checks; node tools/web_smoke.js; pio test -e native (231)
tasks.result: Codex stopped mid-work on a usage limit and left two things unfinished. The CSS positioned the error banner from --toolbar-height with a 240px fallback and nothing ever set that variable, so on a laptop the banner floated a quarter of the way down the page - and since the banner was moved below the toolbar precisely because it was covering the emergency stop, the offset being right is a safety property. app.js now measures the toolbar and re-measures it on resize and through a ResizeObserver, because the toolbar changes height without the window changing size.
