tasks.title: The IMU fault is reproducible: a power cycle fixes it, any software reset breaks it
tasks.test: imu_only over USB after a power cycle; then the wifi firmware; then an OTA
tasks.result: With the battery out and USB as the only supply, unplugging the cable for fifteen seconds is a complete power-down. After one, the standalone tool reported accuracy 3/3, heading uncertainty 1.9 degrees and a 47 uT field - the magnetometer was never the problem. The main firmware then came up with the IMU alive as well. A later over-the-air update, which is a software reset, killed it again: imu_calib_result -100. The sensor's reset line is not wired, so a reboot leaves it streaming and the handshake runs against a transfer already in progress. Every flash therefore needs a power cycle after it, and that is now a stated fact rather than a suspicion.

tasks.title: Re-enabling reports after a sensor reset stalled the control loop for 178 ms
tasks.test: loop_us sampled over two minutes before and after
tasks.result: Every time the BNO085 reset itself, update() re-asked for all four reports inline. Each enableReport is a feature command that waits on the sensor, so the set of them held the 100 Hz control loop: measured at 18, 87, 147 and 178 milliseconds, which is seventeen missed control periods, repeating five times a minute while the sensor was unstable. The reports are now re-asked one per tick - all four back within four control periods, shorter than the gap the reset itself caused. Measured after: 0.56 ms, from a worst case of 178 ms. This is the third time this project has learned that a recovery attempt must not stall the loop, and the first two lessons were written down in CLAUDE.md while this path went unlooked-at.

tasks.title: The dashboard reported a dead IMU as 'ok'
tasks.test: imu_calib_result reads -100 on a board whose IMU never started
tasks.result: imu_calib_result carried the result of the last calibration COMMAND and started at 0, which decodes as 'ok'. On a board where no calibration had ever been run and the IMU had never opened, the web therefore said the IMU's last operation was fine. Two screens disagreed - the standalone tool said the handshake failed on every attempt, the dashboard said everything was fine - and the dashboard was reading a field that had never been written. It now reports the driver's own diagnosis whenever the driver has not started. Also added: enableReport()'s return value was never checked, so 'the sensor refused every report' was indistinguishable from 'the sensor is fine'; that has its own code now, -104, because -103 was already taken.

tasks.title: The web made readable again, and made to fit every screen
tasks.test: node tools/web_smoke.js; python3 tools/qc.py
tasks.result: Stability had been bought at the cost of legibility, which is not a trade worth making. The health pills were stacked onto two lines and are back to one, with the ESP32 pill saying whether the board is there rather than printing an age in seconds - the number moved to the tooltip. The sensor chips had been squeezed into seven columns until every label was an ellipsis; they are two, three or four columns by screen width now, with a constant label and a fixed glyph track. The tab row is centred. The duplicate START button in the Mission card is gone - the big blue one at the top is the only one. Map zoom now runs from 0.02 to 600 px/m and the grid uses a 1-2-5 ladder from 0.1 m, so a courtyard or a dormitory car park has a usable scale; it used to stop at 5 m and in practice sat at 20. Four responsive tiers rather than one: phone, large phone, tablet, and a desktop capped at 1500px.

tasks.title: Board parameters can be written and pulled as a set
tasks.test: node tools/web_smoke.js
tasks.result: Two settings tabs exist because there are two places a setting can live, and nothing said so. The robot tab now states outright that it is the board's own memory, that the Settings tab is this PC's, and that writing is not a flash - it goes over the live link into NVS and takes effect at once. Reload is now 'Pull from robot', and 'Write all to robot' sends every field that differs from what the board reported, one at a time so a refusal can name the parameter it refused.

tasks.title: Cutting USB power from the PC is not possible on this machine
tasks.test: uhubctl
tasks.result: Asked for, and it cannot be done here. uhubctl is installed and reports 'No compatible devices detected' - no hub on this machine supports per-port power switching. A USB port reset or a driver unbind does not cut VBUS, so the sensor stays powered through both. A uhubctl-compatible powered hub between the PC and the board would make it possible, and would let the power cycle after every flash happen without anyone walking over to the robot.

tasks.title: The Wi-Fi radio was browning out the IMU
tasks.test: reset counter over 165 s, before and after
tasks.result: The BNO085 reset itself constantly and lost its calibration each time - 34 resets in 68 seconds at worst - and every symptom pointed at the sensor or the I2C bus. The comparison that settled it fell out of debugging something else: the standalone IMU tool is the same board, sensor and bus with no Wi-Fi, and it ran for minutes with zero resets at a steady 3/3. The radio was the only variable. An ESP32 transmit burst at 20 dBm is a few hundred milliamps, and on USB alone with no battery holding the rail up that browns out a sensor sharing 3V3. Transmit power is 13 dBm now: one reset in 165 seconds, accuracy steady at 3/3, and the IMU survived an over-the-air update without a power cycle for the first time. The proper fix is a battery or bulk capacitance on the sensor supply, after which the power can go back up.

tasks.title: The magnetometer-referenced report will not stream in MODE_BOTH, and no rate change fixes it
tasks.test: report rates at game 100 Hz and at 50 Hz, with resets under control
tasks.result: Halving the game rotation vector was tried, measured as worse, and that measurement was worthless - the radio was browning the sensor out at the time and the reset storm swamped everything. Re-run with the radio turned down it helps the fast reports and does nothing for the slow one: gyro 48-72 to 72-83 Hz, accel 33-49 to 39-46, loop 2.8-9.3 ms to 1.1-6.9 - and the magnetometer-referenced vector stayed at 0.0-0.5 Hz against the 10 asked for. So it is not bandwidth and no rate will fix it: MODE_BOTH asks the BNO085 for two fusions and gets one. The halved rate is kept for the reports that do arrive. It costs little - this is the THIRD absolute heading source, behind GPS course and the QMC5883L, and the QMC5883L works.

tasks.title: The web made legible again after the stability work overshot
tasks.test: node tools/web_smoke.js; python3 tools/qc.py
tasks.result: Stability had been bought by stacking the health pills onto two lines, squeezing seven status chips into columns too narrow for their labels, and moving HDOP into a tooltip - all stable, all unreadable. Pills are one line again with the ESP32 one showing the live age and, when the link drops, how long it has been gone. Chips have short labels and a fixed glyph track with the full wording in the tooltip. HDOP is back in the GPS pill. The control loop is back on the top bar as its own pill. START returned to the Mission card where the waypoints are, and the duplicate at the top is gone. The View and Help bar is centred like the tabs. The magnetometer chip is amber rather than red when it is calibrated but its report is not arriving, because those are different faults with different fixes.

tasks.title: An IMU diagnostic that misreported what it measured
tasks.test: node tools/web_smoke.js
tasks.result: The IMU report-rate verdict had two outcomes - all fine, and bus full - so everything else fell through to 'no reports arriving at all'. It printed exactly that while the gyro, game vector and accelerometer were plainly arriving at 5 Hz each. There are four outcomes now: all delivering, nothing at all, only the slow report starving, and everything arriving but far below what was asked. They have different causes and different fixes, and a diagnostic that misreports the thing it exists to measure is worse than none because it gets believed.

tasks.title: Manual driving holds its heading instead of curving
tasks.test: six new host tests; 237 pass
tasks.result: Manual driving was open loop end to end: the jog buttons produced a speed and a turn rate, those became two PWM numbers, and nothing ever compared where the robot pointed with where it had been pointing. Two motors are never identical - this robot's measured diode drops differ by 0.09 V and its drivers are not matched - so forward drove an arc and the operator had to keep tapping a turn button to fight it. Commanding straight now latches the heading and the heading PID trims the wheel difference to hold it; a turn command releases the hold and re-latches on release, so steering stays direct. The correction is clamped at MANUAL_HOLD_MAX_PWM because it is a trim and not a controller - a hold that can out-pull the person holding the button is worse than no hold. Six tests pin it, including one that proves the trim can never reverse a wheel however long the error is held.

tasks.title: The documentation swept for everything changed in this session
tasks.files: docs/hardware.md, docs/topics.md, docs/architecture.md, docs/calibration.md, docs/running.md, docs/web_ui.md, docs/acceptance.md, docs/tuning.md, README.md, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md
tasks.test: python3 tools/qc.py doc-drift checks
tasks.result: Asked for, and rightly: a lot had changed and the docs still described the old behaviour, which is worse than no documentation because it gets believed. Swept: telemetry 56 to 61 fields and the four new report-rate fields documented; the host test count to 237; the I2C bus back to 400 kHz with the reason the earlier 100 kHz measurement was worthless; the Wi-Fi brown-out and WIFI_TX_POWER; that the BNO085 runs one fusion and never two; the automatic calibration save; the -104 result code and that imu_calib_result now reports the driver's own diagnosis; the loop pill and the map's 1000 km to 1 m zoom range; and manual heading hold in the architecture, acceptance and tuning pages. One passage written earlier in the same session was itself wrong by the end of it - it still blamed bus saturation for the starved magnetometer report, which the later measurements disproved - and has been corrected rather than left to mislead.

tasks.title: Manual driving closes the speed loop as well as the heading one
tasks.test: three more host tests; 240 pass
tasks.result: Manual speed was a feed-forward and nothing else: the requested speed became a PWM and no one checked what came out, so the same request meant one speed on a fresh battery and another on a flat one, up a slope or on carpet. The web page had been promising 'the robot drives at exactly the speed set above' the whole time, which was not true, and that line now says what the firmware actually does. The loop closes only when the fused speed was measured INDEPENDENTLY of the motors - GPS, or IMU acceleration. With neither, the estimator falls back to the motor model, which is computed from the very PWM being set, so a loop closed on it compares the output with itself, learns nothing, and winds its integral up chasing an error that by construction cannot close - on carpet that means the robot accelerating because the model believes it is going slower than it is. A test drives the estimator into model-only and asserts the loop refuses to close.

tasks.title: Manual straight-line driving measured on the floor
tasks.test: drive forward and backward 6 s at 0.18 m/s, record heading drift
tasks.result: First run drifted 4.7 degrees with the correction reading zero on every sample - that was the test harness, not the firmware: the HTTP command loop was slower than the 500 ms watchdog, so the robot kept being stopped and the hold kept re-latching at the current heading, which meant the error could never grow. Driven properly at 20 Hz the hold works: corrections of 13 to 65 PWM and drift down to 3.9 degrees forward and 1.6 degrees backward over six seconds. Also found by the same run: the fused speed read -0.36 m/s while the robot drove forwards, which is what led to the IMU mounting.

tasks.title: The IMU is mounted backwards and the firmware did not know
tasks.result: The sensor's printed X arrow points at the REAR of the robot. IMU_ACC_FORWARD_SIGN was +1 and IMU_YAW_OFFSET_DEG was 0, so the estimator was fed forward acceleration negated and believed the robot accelerated backwards whenever it drove forwards. Nothing reported an error - the number was simply wrong, and plausible. It was blamed on integration drift for an afternoon, and it is why the manual speed loop surged when it was allowed to close on IMU-backed speed. Both constants now say the sensor faces the rear, the geometry parameter defaults from the same constant rather than being a second copy, and qc.py refuses the combination where they disagree: half-fixing this is worse than not fixing it, because a heading squared up while the acceleration still points backwards looks right.

tasks.title: The compass and the IMU now check each other, and either can carry on alone
tasks.files: firmware/src/estimator/state_estimator.h, firmware/src/main.cpp, Telemetry.msg, telemetry.py, web/{index.html,app.js}, docs/architecture.md, docs/topics.md
tasks.test: six new estimator tests; 246 pass
tasks.result: The heading chain was a priority order - GPS course, then the compass, then the BNO085 magnetometer - which says which source to prefer but not whether the preferred one is telling the truth. The compass and the BNO085 magnetometer are both absolute and both fooled by the same things: a motor drawing current, a steel bench, rebar in a floor. The IMU's fused yaw is fooled by none of them because it comes from the gyroscope, and although it drifts slowly it is the honest one over the seconds a disturbance lasts. Every absolute reference is now checked against it before being believed, and heading_innov_deg and heading_gated report the disagreement on the dashboard so it can be seen rather than guessed at. Measured on this robot before the change: the compass moved 9.5 degrees in 0.3 s while the gyroscope reported about 1 deg/s, and applied blind that step went into the heading and the manual hold steered to it. Two details stop the gate causing worse problems than it solves, and both have tests: the FIRST alignment is never gated, because before it there is nothing to disagree with and gating it would mean the robot never finds north; and a disagreement that outlasts agree_recover_s is accepted anyway, because a gate that can never give up locks out a correct sensor for ever if the gyro really has drifted. Losing either sensor still falls through to the other, which was already true and is now tested.

tasks.title: The BNO085's own integrated orientation is the backbone, and now it actually arrives
tasks.test: pio test -e native (246); pio run -e wifi
tasks.result: The backbone already WAS the sensor's own fused orientation rather than a gyro rate integrated in the control loop - that part was right. What was wrong is that it was barely arriving: MODE_BOTH asks the BNO085 for two fusions, it delivers one, and the game rotation vector had been starving at 2 to 7 Hz against the 100 asked for. Both things this robot reads from the sensor come from that one report - the heading backbone, and the roll and pitch that tilt-compensate the QMC5883L - so a starved rotation vector was quietly making the compass wrong on slopes as well. The mode is now IMU_REPORT_MODE in config/imu.h, set to the game vector alone, and it is deliberately separate from HEADING_SOURCE: those answer different questions, and deriving one from the other meant neither could be changed without disturbing the other. The game vector is the right one to keep because it is immune to magnets - north comes from the compass and the GPS course, both cross-checked against it - whereas the magnetometer-referenced vector would make the backbone out of the sensor this robot trusts least, the magnetometer sitting beside the motors.

tasks.title: The agent address is discovered, never assumed
tasks.test: boot log shows mDNS resolution instead of a hand-set address
tasks.result: The board printed '[agent] using 192.168.100.74 (set by hand)' on every boot - an address from a network it had not been on for hours - then adopted the beacon a moment later. A hand-set address lives in NVS and survives every reboot, so one typed on a network the robot has since left goes on being tried for ever. Any agent address, hand-set or compiled in, is now ignored when it is off the subnet the board actually joined: an address outside the board's own network cannot be reached directly, so preferring it over discovery is not a judgement call, it is always wrong. The boot log now reads '[agent] mannaja.local -> 192.168.12.1 (mDNS)' with no hand-set address at all.

tasks.title: One Wi-Fi radio cannot host the robot's hotspot and stay joined to a 5 GHz router
tasks.test: uptime with the uplink up versus down
tasks.result: The PC hosts the robot's hotspot on ap0 (2.4 GHz channel 1) using the SAME radio, phy#0, that is joined to a 5 GHz router on channel 149. One radio cannot be on two bands, so it time-slices and the hotspot stalls for seconds at a time. Every direct measurement of the link looked perfect - minus 54 dBm, zero tx retries, zero tx failed - and the micro-ROS session died every 40 to 60 seconds anyway. Measured both ways: with the uplink brought down the board reached 348 s of uptime; with it back up, 40 s again. This is an environment problem, not a firmware one, and it is blocked on a decision only the operator can make - put the robot on the same router the PC uses and run no hotspot, give the PC a wired or tethered uplink, or force the AP onto the uplink's channel. The client liveliness timeout was also raised from 1000 ms to 10000 ms along the way, which was a genuine fault of its own but did not fix this.

tasks.title: The board still resets itself about once a minute, cause not yet proven
tasks.test: esp_reset_reason across several cycles, with the radio conflict removed
tasks.result: Not solved, and recorded as unsolved. The board publishes for roughly 20 s, the host stops hearing it for about 50 s while the board's own uptime keeps counting, then the board resets. esp_reset_reason reports ESP_RST_SW, so something calls esp_restart deliberately; the only such call in this firmware is the agent self-heal, which logs first and that log was never seen - though the console is unreadable at present, so the absence proves little. Ruled out with measurements: heap is flat at 157-172 kB so there is no leak; the control loop runs 2.4 to 9 ms against a 10 ms period; imu_resets stays at 1; RF is clean. The USB console reads 548 KB/s of one repeating fragment, which is 48 times what 115200 baud can carry and therefore cannot be arriving in real time - it survived a full USB re-enumeration, and the board is demonstrably running normally while it happens, so it is an adapter artefact and not the firmware. I briefly reported it as a firmware bug before checking that the board was still publishing; it was.

tasks.title: The access point was evicting the robot, not the robot disconnecting
tasks.test: count of 'deauthenticated due to inactivity' per five minutes
tasks.result: hostapd logged the ESP32 as deauthenticated due to inactivity every half minute, it re-associated, and the micro-ROS session died each time. The board was never idle - it publishes ten times a second. hostapd judges a station inactive when its OWN null-data poll goes unanswered, and on a radio also joined to a 5 GHz network as a client those polls are the first thing lost. Measured: 9 evictions in five minutes with the uplink up against 1 with it down. The hotspot is linux-wifi-hotspot (create_ap), which exposes none of the relevant hostapd keys, so the script is patched to emit skip_inactivity_poll=1, ap_max_inactivity=3600 and disassoc_low_ack=0, and the config gained IEEE80211N=1 with HT_CAPAB=[SHORT-GI-20] so frames spend less airtime. Dated backups sit beside both files. Not yet confirmed on hardware: the hotspot was off when the first measurement was attempted, so that reading was void and is recorded as void.

tasks.title: IMU accuracy stuck at 0/3, and the automatic calibration save with it
tasks.test: pio test -e native (246); accuracy follows the running rotation vector
tasks.result: Reported as 'IMU mag back to 0, yesterday it was 2-3 and stable'. Correct, and it was a regression I introduced: switching IMU_REPORT_MODE to the game vector alone stopped the magnetometer-referenced report being enabled, and the ONLY writer of accuracy_ lived inside that report's handler. So accuracy could never leave 0. Three things followed from one line: the dashboard showed a permanently uncalibrated sensor, imu_magnetometer_missing was raised for ever, and the automatic calibration save added the day before - which waits for 3/3 - became unreachable code. The game vector reports its own 0-3 confidence for the accelerometer-and-gyro fusion it actually runs, so accuracy now follows whichever vector is enabled, and the estimator only raises the missing-magnetometer flag when that report was asked for in the first place. A magnetometer nobody asked for cannot be missing.

tasks.title: The link is fixed: the access point was evicting the robot
tasks.test: deauth count per five minutes, and uptime
tasks.result: Confirmed on hardware after the hotspot was restarted with the patched config. One deauth in five minutes against a baseline of nine, and the board ran 1072 seconds - eighteen minutes - with telemetry age at 0.0 throughout, against a previous best of 40 to 60 seconds. This is the fault behind every 'the ESP32 keeps disconnecting' report on this project: hostapd was evicting a station that publishes ten times a second for being inactive, because its own null-data polls were being lost on a radio shared with a 5 GHz client connection. The robot was never the one disconnecting.

tasks.title: The IMU drain budget was starving the rotation vector
tasks.test: delivered report rates at 2 ms and at 4 ms
tasks.result: The 2 ms per-tick budget added to bound the control loop was itself the reason the BNO085's fused orientation was arriving a few times a second. Events drain in arrival order, so a budget that runs out part way through starves whatever sits at the back, and that was always the rotation vector. Measured at 2 ms: 113 of the 200 reports a second asked for, with the rotation vector at 0 to 6 Hz of its 50 while the gyroscope got 65 of 100. At 4 ms: 168 to 187 of 200, and the rotation vector 43 to 49 of 50. The loop now runs 4.6 to 9.3 ms against a 10 ms period, which is close enough to the ceiling that this is the first number to reduce if control periods start being missed.

tasks.title: The Topics page could not show any topic the robot publishes
tasks.test: GET /api/topic?name=/gps_localize/imu/data returns data; three QC checks
tasks.result: Reported as '/gps_localize/imu/data shows nothing, it just waits'. The echo created its subscription with a plain depth of 10, and a plain depth carries RELIABLE with it. Every topic the firmware publishes is BEST_EFFORT, and DDS does not connect a RELIABLE reader to a BEST_EFFORT writer - it never matches and reports nothing anywhere. So the page waited for ever on precisely the topics someone opens it to look at: imu/data, telemetry, odom, gps/fix. This is the same QoS asymmetry already in the project rules, reached from the other direction. The echo now asks the graph what each publisher offers and mirrors its reliability and durability, which is what a generic tool pointed at an arbitrary topic should do. Measured after: imu/data 19.5 Hz with data, telemetry 9.5 Hz, gps/fix 5.0 Hz. A plain integer depth is the trap - it reads as 'queue 10' and silently carries a reliability policy with it.

tasks.title: /gps_localize/odom is published by the firmware and never arrives
tasks.test: ros2 topic hz /gps_localize/odom; the [odom] console line
tasks.result: Not solved. publishOdom() runs every cycle and the topic shows one publisher, but nothing is delivered - confirmed over twelve seconds with ros2 directly and through the web echo, both after the QoS fix that repaired the other four topics. rcl_publish's return was being discarded by RCSOFTCHECK, which is right for a publisher that misses the odd cycle and wrong for one that has never worked; it now records the code and prints it once per change. Reading that needs the USB console, which is currently unusable - the adapter delivers 548 KB/s of binary, 48 times what 115200 can carry, with no readable strings in six megabytes. Odometry is by far the largest message the board sends, two 36-wide float64 covariance arrays and about 700 bytes before framing against a 1024-byte transport MTU, so a size or buffer refusal is the leading suspicion and is recorded as a suspicion rather than a finding. Nothing on the robot depends on it: the web reads /odom/gps from the host node and odom_x/odom_y from telemetry, so this costs external consumers such as rviz and bag files. 2026-09-12, root cause found without the console: a BEST_EFFORT subscriber on the host counted 0.0 Hz on /odom while /imu/data ran at 20.1 Hz over the same link, and rclpy's own serializer puts Odometry at 724 bytes against Imu 324, Telemetry 260 and NavSatFix 125. The generated libmicroros headers show RMW_UXRCE_TRANSPORT_CUSTOM with UXR_CONFIG_CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU 512: micro_ros_platformio's Wi-Fi transport is a custom transport, and colcon.meta had raised only UCLIENT_UDP_TRANSPORT_MTU, which this build never uses. A best-effort stream cannot fragment, so the one message over 512 bytes was refused every time. Fix: UCLIENT_CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU=1024. Verified after wiping and rebuilding libmicroros (515 s) and reflashing: the generated header now reads UXR_CONFIG_CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU 1024, /odom arrives at 10.0 Hz (PUB_ODOM_DIV 10) with frame odom -> base_link, /imu/data stays at 20.0 Hz, and the real-time baseline holds: tools/loop_probe.py 45 gave 0 of 900 IMU publishes late, gap p99 57.3 ms, loop_us p99 5407 us, all 450 telemetry frames. Cost: RAM 27.7% -> 33.0% (+17.4 KB of larger stream buffers). docs/topics.md claimed 20 Hz; the divider gives 10 and 10 was measured. tools/qc.py now fails when the custom-transport MTU in colcon.meta is below the largest firmware message plus framing, and its libmicroros freshness check counts colcon.meta as an input - proven by setting the MTU back to 512, which QC rejected.

tasks.title: The caster geometry described a robot this is not
tasks.test: pio run -e wifi; 86 parameters in the manifest; node tools/web_smoke.js
tasks.result: The geometry named one caster at the front and one at the rear. This robot has TWO casters, both at the front, with the driven wheels at the rear. A name that describes the wrong machine is worse than no name because it is read as if it were true - somebody measuring 'rear caster' would have walked to the back of the robot and found a drive wheel. Renamed throughout to caster.fl and caster.fr, with the sign convention spelled out on the right-hand one the way it already is for the right wheel, and the web UI now labels the drive wheels as REAR so the two halves of the layout are stated rather than assumed. The parameter count is unchanged at 86 - the same eleven values per caster, describing the right parts.

tasks.title: A map-picked destination was thrown away on stop
tasks.test: curl /api/waypoints after a stop; the saved runtime file
tasks.result: Waypoints added from the list or from 'add here' were already saved and already survived a restart - that part worked. What did not was a point picked on the map: it lived only in memory as temp_target and stopping threw it away, so closing the browser or rebooting lost it and the next session started with nothing to drive to. Somebody who has just driven somewhere worth going has already decided it is worth keeping. STOP now appends that point to the saved list before clearing it as a target, skipping anything within about a metre of a point already there so stopping twice in the same place does not fill the list with copies. The shipped default is 18.7889332, 98.9553871 rather than the Bangkok pair, and the runtime list was set to it.

tasks.title: Drive forward and turn at the same time, by joystick and by keyboard
tasks.files: web/{index.html,style.css,app.js}, firmware/src/control/drive_controller.h, firmware/config/control.h, firmware/src/params/param_table.h, firmware/src/main.cpp, docs/{web_ui.md,tuning.md}
tasks.test: three new drive tests, 249 pass; node tools/web_smoke.js
tasks.result: The firmware had always taken speed and yaw rate in the same command - linear.x and angular.z of one Twist - so driving an arc was never a control limit. It was the interface: the arrow pad sends one axis at a time, and the keyboard handler remembered a single key, so pressing W then A replaced forward with turn and releasing either stopped the robot outright. A curve had to be driven by alternating two buttons, which gives a zig-zag. There is now a joystick on the dashboard - one gesture, both axes, magnitude proportional to how far the knob is pushed and scaled by the same speed limit the buttons use, so it cannot become a second hidden throttle - and the keyboard holds a SET of keys and sums them, so W+A is forward-and-left. AUTO already drove and steered together for any heading error under 45 degrees; above that it stops and turns, because arcing from 90 degrees off covers about half as much ground again. That threshold is now the live parameter control.spin_above_deg: 180 means it never stops to turn, which is smoother in an open field and worse in a corridor.

tasks.title: After a turn the robot kicked back the other way before driving on
tasks.test: two new drive tests; 251 pass
tasks.result: Reported from the robot: release the turn, and it turns back a little before going forward. The heading hold latched the instant the turn command stopped, and the FUSED heading lags the robot - the compass is eased in over seconds and the IMU's own fusion has its own delay - so what it latched was where the robot had been a moment earlier. The hold then did exactly what it was told and steered back to that stale heading. A rate threshold on its own would not have fixed it either, because the estimate is still catching up for a moment after the rotation itself has stopped, so both conditions are required: the yaw rate under MANUAL_HOLD_SETTLE_DPS for MANUAL_HOLD_SETTLE_S. Until it latches there is no correction at all - both wheels drive equally and the operator's last command stands - which is pinned by its own test, because a half-applied hold would be the same bug wearing a different face.

tasks.title: Theme chosen in Settings, and the declination named the wrong city
tasks.test: node tools/web_smoke.js
tasks.result: The page followed the device and there was no way to override it, which is wrong in both directions: a phone set to dark is still hard to read in direct sunlight, and a laptop set to light glares in a dark workshop. Three states now - auto, light, dark - in the Settings tab rather than the toolbar, because it is set once and the toolbar is reserved for what changes while driving. The ordering is the load-bearing part: a media query and an attribute rule at the same specificity are decided by source order, so the [data-theme] rules come after the media query and the dark tokens are restated rather than left to :root, or choosing dark on a light device would silently do nothing. The choice lives in localStorage, because it belongs to the screen looking at the robot rather than the robot - a phone in sun and a laptop indoors want opposite answers from the same machine at the same moment. web_smoke caught a real omission on the first run: its fake DOM had no removeAttribute, which the real one has, so the harness was extended rather than the code bent around it. Separately, mag_declination_deg said 0.6 and was labelled Bangkok while this robot works in Chiang Mai, where it is about +0.3 - a third of a degree, far smaller than the compass's own error, so this is tidiness rather than a fix, but a number naming the wrong city invites misplaced trust.

tasks.title: Fusion bug: a mis-paste reset the fix quality on every accepted fix
tasks.test: python3 tools/live_probe.py; python3 tools/qc.py
tasks.result: A block of tuning constants had been pasted into the middle of fuse_correct, and two lines of it were not constants at all: self.hdop = 9.9 and self.satellites = 0 ran on EVERY accepted fix. gps_sigma_m() reads both, so immediately after each correction it returned max(0.5, 9.9*2.0)*2.0 = 39.6 m instead of about 2.6 m. Two consequences, both silent: the Kalman gain put almost no weight on GPS, so the estimate ran on dead reckoning, and the outlier gate opened to 3*hypot(1.5, 39.6) = 119 m, which accepts anything at all. The filter was neither trusting GPS nor rejecting bad fixes. Removed; the constants are declared once in __init__ where they always belonged.

tasks.title: Waypoint arrival survives the receiver's own noise
tasks.files: gps_localize/waypoint_nav.py, config/nav.yaml, test/test_arrival.py, docs/{tuning,safety,acceptance}.md, tools/{qc,_ui_stub}.py, web/app.js
tasks.test: python3 gps_localize_ws/src/gps_localize/test/test_arrival.py
tasks.result: The robot drove to a waypoint twice and never declared it reached. arrive_radius_m was 1.0 m; measured on the real robot, stationary outdoors on 8 satellites at HDOP 1.3, the fix scattered 1.56 m median and 4.86 m worst. The radius was below the receiver's own noise, so arrival was decided by luck. Widening it alone would have traded never-arriving for arriving early, because a single noisy sample can land inside a 2.5 m circle from 4 m away - so both halves went in: a hard floor of 2.0 m that ignores any smaller configured value, a radius that also grows with the fusion's reported sigma so a degraded fix under trees still finishes, and a dwell requirement that the robot stay inside for arrive_hold_s while standing still. Standing still during the dwell matters: at that range the remaining distance is mostly noise, and steering on it drives the robot back out of the circle and restarts the timer. 9 tests, including the measured scatter pattern replayed against a robot standing on the point.

tasks.title: A waypoint can name the heading to face on arrival
tasks.test: python3 gps_localize_ws/src/gps_localize/test/test_arrival.py
tasks.result: A waypoint was a place only. It is now a place and, optionally, a direction to be facing once the robot gets there - which is what anything happening AT the point depends on: driving onto a dock, lining up with a gate, aiming a camera. New ALIGN state: the robot arrives first and then turns on the spot, because this robot steers by driving and any attempt to arrive already facing the right way costs a curved approach that lands it somewhere else. No firmware change was needed - linear.y = 1.0 already means rotate to this heading and stop, with the firmware's own tolerance and settle time. A turn that cannot be completed within align_timeout_s advances the mission anyway and says so: the robot HAS arrived, and stopping everything over the last few degrees would be the worse failure. Blank means any direction, and that had to be handled explicitly on both sides - Number('') is 0, which would silently order the robot to face north.

tasks.title: GPS reported as a missing sensor while the robot navigated on it
tasks.test: pio test -e native (254 cases)
tasks.result: The web UI drew the GPS sensor as a red cross on 7 satellites at HDOP 1.8 - a real, usable fix the robot was navigating on at that moment. One flag was answering two different questions. gps_ok is a SPEED gate, and its thresholds are named for it (GPS_MIN_SATS_FOR_SPEED, GPS_MAX_HDOP_FOR_SPEED 1.5) because a marginal fix reports plausible-looking nonsense ground speeds - that bar is right for the speed filter. It is the wrong bar for HEALTH_NO_GPS, which is a statement about the SENSOR. Split: gps_fix_ok is fresh + a real fix + at least 4 satellites, with no HDOP term at all, because poor geometry makes a position less precise rather than absent and the HDOP value already travels in telemetry for anything that needs to weigh it. Three native tests hold the split, including one proving the speed path was not loosened. Built; waiting on the board to be on the network to flash.

tasks.title: Wi-Fi signal strength at the robot, on the top bar
tasks.test: python3 tools/port_qc.py --static-only . (64 telemetry fields match)
tasks.result: Telemetry field 63, wifi_rssi_dbm, beside the link, battery, GPS and loop pills. It is the number that separates 'the firmware has stopped' from 'it drove out of range', and without it that guess was being made from the failure alone - which is how weeks went into the IMU before anyone looked at the radio. It is the signal at the ROBOT, not at the browser: a phone can sit beside the router while the robot is at the far end of the garden. The firmware sends 0 rather than WiFi.RSSI() when not associated, because that API returns a plausible-looking negative number in that state which would read as a weak link rather than no link. Adding the field meant rebuilding libmicroros - and the cached libmicroros/ directory has to be deleted as well as build/, or the generated header keeps the old message and the build fails on a missing member. Built; waiting on the board to flash.

tasks.test: python3 tools/qc.py (web_smoke)
tasks.result: The theme buttons sat loose at the top of the Settings tab, above the group selector, which put a setting of this browser among the robot's. They now appear with the rest of the 'เว็บ / Web' group and are hidden otherwise. They stay outside #cfgForm on purpose: renderConfig empties that element on every group change, which would destroy the buttons and the listeners bound to them at startup. tasks.title: The GPS quality settings only moved half the robot
tasks.test: pio test -e native (254); GET /api/params shows 90 with live values from the board
tasks.result: Changing the minimum satellites and maximum HDOP on the Settings page changed the HOST's navigation gate (nav.min_satellites / nav.max_hdop, used by waypoint_nav.fix_usable) and nothing on the board: GPS_MIN_SATS_FOR_SPEED and GPS_MAX_HDOP_FOR_SPEED were plain #defines read straight into main.cpp, while gps.stale_ms beside them was a proper parameter. So half the setting worked and the half that decides whether the receiver's velocity is believed silently kept its compiled-in 6 and 1.5. All three are parameters now, including the new gps.min_sats_fix. Two traps on the way: PARAM_COUNT is a hand-maintained size that has to be bumped or the array will not compile, and gen_param_manifest.py parses one string literal per row - a help text split across concatenated lines is skipped in silence, which showed up as 'PARAM_COUNT says 90 but 87 rows parsed'. Both were caught by checks that already existed.

tasks.title: The pill row wrapped when a sixth pill was added
tasks.test: python3 tools/qc.py
tasks.result: The Wi-Fi signal pill dropped onto a second line because .pills had grid-template-columns: repeat(5, minmax(0,1fr)) - a hand-counted track list with nothing tying it to how many pills the HTML contains. Replaced with grid-auto-flow: column and grid-auto-columns: minmax(0,1fr), which takes the count from the children and cannot fall out of step; the phone breakpoint puts the flow back to rows so six pills wrap three-and-three instead of scrolling off. The QC check that should have caught it was satisfied by the mere PRESENCE of grid-template-columns, so it watched the row wrap and said nothing - it now accepts either spelling and rejects auto-fit/auto-fill, which genuinely re-flow.

tasks.title: Changing Telemetry.msg silently breaks the link with an unflashed board
tasks.test: ros2 topic echo /gps_localize/telemetry against a board on old firmware
tasks.result: After adding wifi_rssi_dbm the board linked normally - session established, participant and five subscribers created, ping 10 ms - and no telemetry arrived at all. ros2 topic info showed one publisher and five subscriptions with matching type NAMES, so every ordinary check looked healthy; the board was still serialising the 63-field message the host no longer expected. Worth knowing because the symptom points at the network or the firmware rather than at the message: the board was reachable, the agent log was clean, and the only evidence was silence on a topic that appeared to be connected. Flashing over Wi-Fi fixed it immediately. Also confirmed on the way: the 90-second session drops were the board rebooting, and the reason it was absent earlier was simply that the battery was off.

tasks.title: The hidden attribute does nothing on an element a class gives display to
tasks.test: python3 tools/qc.py
tasks.result: The theme row was moved into the Web settings group and appeared under every group instead. The toggle was correct - themeRow.hidden = true, and the DOM showed hidden="" - but the element is a .row, .row sets display:flex, and an author rule beats the browser's own [hidden]{display:none} at equal specificity. So the attribute was set and the row stayed on screen, with nothing anywhere reporting a problem. The project already had .hidden carrying !important for exactly this, and that is what it uses now. QC gained a check that FAILS rather than notes: any element toggled through the hidden attribute in app.js must not have a class that sets display.

tasks.title: Reading the Wi-Fi signal in the control callback cost 85 ms of loop time
tasks.test: loop_us sampled at 2 Hz for 45 s, before and after, same board and same room
tasks.result: Asked whether the new signal reading was costing loop time. It was, and by much more than expected. WiFi.RSSI() is not a memory read: it calls esp_wifi_sta_get_ap_info(), which takes the Wi-Fi driver's lock and can wait on the radio task mid-transmission - and it was being called inside controlCallback, where the PID, the safety chain and the estimator run. Moved to once a second in loop(), where a wait costs nothing, and the four string-keyed params.get() calls in the same callback were cached alongside it (the registry resolves a key by walking the table with strcmp, so each one was up to ninety compares, ten thousand times a second, for a value a person changes twice a day). Measured over 90 samples before and after: median 8747 -> 5465 us, p90 94046 -> 8880 us, max 169745 -> 108494 us, and the IMU game-rotation rate rose from 29.7 to 38.1 Hz because the loop was no longer stealing its service time. The p90 collapse is the radio lock. A 108 ms spike remains and has a different cause, still unfound.

tasks.title: Keep the Wi-Fi signal reading off the real-time path, or remove it
tasks.test: python3 tools/loop_probe.py 45, A/B under identical power and placement
tasks.result: Asked for: the robot must run in real time the way it did before the signal pill was added; keep the signal only if it costs the control loop nothing, otherwise delete it. loop_us alone cannot answer that - it only times controlCallback, so a stall in loop() delays the callback without lengthening it. tools/loop_probe.py measures both: loop_us from every telemetry frame, and gaps between the firmware's own /imu/data stamps, which expose a late control loop on the robot's clock rather than the network's. Result: KEEP IT. Three runs of tools/loop_probe.py 45 on USB power: A (reading once a second in loop()) 16 of 873 late, A2 18 of 875, C (reading compiled out with -DWIFI_RSSI_ENABLE=0) 12 of 878 - a difference of about one standard deviation, and loop_us cannot be affected by construction since the read sits outside the callback. More to the point, the stalls were all still there with the reading gone, which is what sent the search on to T205. With T205 in place and the signal still enabled: 0 of 900 late.

tasks.title: Any of Claude, Codex or Gemini/Antigravity can take over when another hits its limit
tasks.test: tools/agent_relay.sh --dry-run lists every agent it can run; a simulated limit moves to the next
tasks.result: Asked for: rotate between three models so the bug work continues when any one of them runs out, because Claude's weekly allowance is nearly spent. Needs a shared state file every agent reads first and updates before it stops, instruction files each tool reads automatically, and a runner that detects a usage-limit failure and moves on. Built: HANDOFF.md (live state, queue, unattended-agent rules, real-time baseline), GEMINI.md, a HANDOFF pointer in AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, a claude wrapper in ~/.local/bin resolving the VS Code extension's binary the way the codex one does, and tools/agent_relay.sh. Proven: claude -p returned RELAY_OK; codex exec returned a REAL usage-limit error ('You've hit your usage limit ... try again at 4:32 AM', exit 1), which the relay's detection matches; simulated limit, chatty-but-healthy and crashing agents were classified limited, idle and failed respectively. Still open: the Gemini CLI is not installed on this PC (Node v12, no npm; it needs Node 20+) - a system install, so it waits for the user.

tasks.title: The agent ping stalled the control loop without showing in loop_us
tasks.test: python3 tools/loop_probe.py 45 on the same firmware with and without a live heartbeat; pio test -e native (254)
tasks.result: rmw_uros_ping_agent(300, 3) ran every 700 ms in loop(), which also spins the executor that fires the 100 Hz control timer, so every ping made the next tick late by a Wi-Fi round trip and a slow one made it late by 50-70 ms. loop_us could not see it - it only times the callback. Now the ping runs only when neither a heartbeat nor a drive command has arrived for a whole period; real traffic through the agent proves the session better than a ping, and silence brings the ping straight back, so lost-agent detection is unchanged and the safety chain still stops the motors on a stale heartbeat by itself. Measured, USB power, idle: before 1.4-2.2% of IMU publishes late, gap p99 ~100 ms, max 105-122 ms, telemetry frames missing (436-439 of 450); after 0 of 900 late, gap p99 55.8 ms, max 61.6 ms, all 450 telemetry frames, and loop_us p99 fell from ~10 ms to 5.2 ms because the IMU no longer builds a backlog during the stall. One wrong turn on the way: ros2 topic hz piped through grep under timeout printed nothing, which read as no heartbeat - it was output buffering, and a counting subscriber showed 7-10 Hz throughout.

tasks.title: The relay drives Antigravity's CLI as the third agent

tasks.result: The user installed Antigravity. It ships a CLI, agy 1.2.1, in ~/.gemini/bin - not on PATH - with a print mode (-p), --dangerously-skip-permissions, --model, --effort and a --print-timeout that defaults to five minutes, far too short for a relay round. agy models lists gemini-3.8-flash-high, the model the user asked for. Smoke test: agy -p returned RELAY_OK, exit 0. The relay's default order is now claude codex agy; agy is resolved from ~/.gemini/bin when it is not on PATH, and its --print-timeout is tied to the relay's own round timeout rather than its five-minute default, which would have cut every real round off mid-task.

tasks.title: Three-way bug hunt: Claude, Codex and Antigravity each report separately
tasks.test: each report exists, names file:line, and nothing in the repository is modified
tasks.result: Asked for: find every bug and problem in the program, write what each model found to its own file, and FIX NOTHING yet. Three independent readers on the same code is the point - the expensive bugs on this project (the radio browning out the IMU, the one-second liveness timeout, the MTU on the wrong transport) were each hidden behind a single wrong assumption, and a reader who does not share it is worth more than more effort inside it. Separate files so the three can be compared rather than blended. Done, nothing fixed. Three reports: claude_found_bug.md (13 findings), gpt_found_bug.md (21, with runnable repros in gpt_found_bug_evidence/), gemini_found_bug.md (20 across six files). Verified no source file was modified - find -newermt over the run window is empty and git status went 93 to 96, exactly the three new report paths. The three agreed on the worst one independently: automatic steering inverts its own feedback in reverse (drive_controller.h:174). Two of three found a crash in T194's own ALIGN code that this session shipped and its author missed: advance() clears align_target and returns without leaving the ALIGN state on an intermediate waypoint, so the next tick calls geo.angle_error_deg(None, heading) and the node that drives the robot dies mid-mission - confirmed by reading waypoint_nav.py:601 against advance(). Two process lessons: codex exec and agy both hang forever on an open stdin (agent_relay.sh already passes </dev/null; a hand-rolled launch did not), and agy -p has a five-minute print timeout that silently returns nothing - telling it to write its report file first and rewrite it after each file reviewed is what made a long review survive.

tasks.title: ALIGN never leaves its state at an intermediate waypoint, killing waypoint_nav
tasks.test: a two-waypoint mission with a heading on the first; the node must survive the advance
tasks.result: Introduced by T194 in this session and missed by its author; found independently by Codex (GPT-003) and Antigravity (4.1). advance() sets align_target to None and returns without set_state for the intermediate-waypoint and loop_waypoints branches, so the state stays ALIGN and the next tick evaluates geo.angle_error_deg(None, self.heading_deg) - a TypeError in the timer callback of the node that drives the robot. Only reachable when a waypoint carries a heading AND another waypoint follows it, which is why the single-point tests passed. NOT FIXED - the user asked for findings only. Fixed: advance() now calls set_state(RUNNING) on the intermediate-waypoint and loop branches. Held by test_nav_guards.py, which also checks the two branches that already worked.

tasks.title: Fix everything the three-way audit found, without breaking what works
tasks.files: waypoint_nav.py, web_server.py, telemetry_split.py, drive_controller.h, safety_manager.h, state_estimator.h, main.cpp, config/*.h, tests
tasks.test: host tests, pio test -e native, tools/qc.py, port_qc, live_probe, loop_probe against the recorded baseline, /odom still 10 Hz
tasks.result: The user asked for all of it fixed and explicitly asked that nothing working now be broken, so each fix is verified against the gates and the recorded real-time baseline rather than assumed. Merged list from claude_found_bug.md, gpt_found_bug.md and gemini_found_bug.md: 24 distinct defects after removing duplicates. Order: host-side crashes and unguarded motion first (no flash), then firmware, then one flash and a re-measurement. HOST HALF DONE AND LIVE: the ALIGN crash, discovery driving on a stale fix, the raw fix clobbering the fused position, NaN manual input reaching the motors, api_turn bypassing the motion gate, motion_blocker ignoring contactor_stuck and battery_soft, the software e-stop latch cleared by a host restart, the stale HOST_EXPECTS_FIRMWARE banner, the dead nav.reverse_allowed setting, and the three web.yaml settings the browser ignored. 58 host tests pass (12 new), QC and the port gate pass apart from the known stale Docker image, live_probe passes, the restarted stack logs nothing. FIRMWARE HALF BUILT BUT NOT FLASHED - the board dropped off the network mid-session so nothing could be verified on hardware: reverse steering sign, zero-speed not ending a spin, reset() leaving a turn running, the manual hold surviving a mode change, an unbounded turn-in-place, the auto speed loop closing on an unmeasured estimate, the contactor check running after the decision it should feed, the update lockout allowing motion, the relay opening a cycle late off stale flags, soft-stop chatter, the heading reference lying when every source is dead, the EKF gated on the speed-grade fix, unsigned GPS speed and course in reverse, OTA accepted mid-rotation, and an INA226 that could never come back. 261 native tests pass (7 new), firmware builds at RAM 33.0% / flash 54.0%. One finding was measured WRONG and reverted - see T210. FLASHED AND PROVEN: firmware version bumped 1.61 -> 1.62 so the OTA is identifiable at all - both images had reported 161, which is why the relay could not prove its own flash landed. The board now reports 1.62 with 6 satellites, HDOP 1.45, battery 12.39 V, no stop reasons and no missing sensors. tools/qc.py gained a check tying HOST_EXPECTS_FIRMWARE to version.h so the pair cannot drift again. Loop timing is unresolved rather than regressed: 5.4-10.9 ms against a 10 ms period, but the 3.2 ms baseline was recorded with no GPS fix and no battery, and the rise was present before the flash. Link churn (8 session rebuilds in 21 minutes, a third of frames lost) is the NAT path between the board's hotspot subnet and the PC's wired LAN, and also predates the flash.

tasks.title: An audit finding that measurement disproved: the EKF covariance floor
tasks.test: pio test -e native, test_ekf_beats_raw_gps_and_dead_reckoning
tasks.result: claude_found_bug.md finding 11 called the 1e-4 covariance floor 'a 1 cm sigma this receiver can never earn' and proposed 0.5 m. Applied, two EKF tests failed. Instrumented the sim rather than adjusting the expectation: final error went to 3.44 m against raw GPS 2.73 m and dead reckoning 0.41 m - the filter became worse than both of its inputs, because a floored covariance keeps the gain high and makes it follow each fix instead of averaging across them. Reverted, with the numbers written into the code beside the floor. The finding was mine, and the tests are what caught it.
